title: Atlas House to the Open Sea: the Draper's Apprentice Who Wrote the Century Before It Happened
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bromley, Atlas House: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Date, birth order and the Atlas House address are confirmed by Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells'. The coordinate given by the chronology lens (51.4028, 0.0148) fell some 300 m south of the site and has been replaced with the Nominatim point for Market Square, Bromley (51.4054, 0.0154), where the blue plaque stands; the geography and afterlife lenses both gave 51.4039, 0.0198, roughly 330 m too far east, and have been reconciled to the same pin.
stops.campa: Joseph Wells sells china and cricket goods from a shop on the Bromley High Street and calls it Atlas House, for the plaster figure straining under the world in its window. Above that shop, on the twenty-first of September, Sarah Neal bears her fourth and last child. They name him Herbert George; the family calls him Bertie. The trade is already failing. His father's real money comes from professional cricket, played for Kent, and his mother will go back into domestic service at Uppark to keep the household standing.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: The blue plaque on Market Square, Bromley, on the wall of what is now a Primark store, marking the site of Atlas House

stops.name: Bromley, 8 South Street: Mrs Knott's dame school
stops.date_confidence: place attested, date not. Wikipedia, 'Bromley' records a marble plaque at 8 South Street marking the site of Mrs Knott's dame school where Wells learned to read and write; no source consulted gives the years he attended. The date here is a placeholder to order the segment and carries no evidential weight.
stops.campa: Before he is old enough for anything else he is walked along South Street to Mrs Knott's dame school, a front room where a woman teaches the neighbourhood children their letters for pennies a week. He learns to read and write there, and it is his whole education until Morley's Academy takes him in 1874. Bromley is a market town on the London coach road, and at home the shop is losing money faster every year. No source records what years he attended, or what was taught in that room beyond the letters.
suggested_refs: The marble plaque at 8 South Street, Bromley, marking the site of the dame school

stops.name: Bromley, the broken leg and Morley's Academy
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' places both the leg injury and his entry to Thomas Morley's Commercial Academy in 1874; it does not date either within the year, and does not say which came first.
stops.campa: He breaks his leg and is laid up for weeks with nothing to do. Books are brought to him, more at once than he has ever had, and he reads through them without stopping. The same year he is entered at Thomas Morley's Commercial Academy on the High Street, a private school that teaches boys bookkeeping and a commercial hand for the counting house. Neither event is dated inside the year and no source says which came first. What Morley's gives him is four years of arithmetic and copperplate, the hand a clerk needs to keep a ledger straight.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: Thomas Morley's Commercial Academy, Bromley High Street

stops.name: Wookey, the National School
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place, contested as to date. Both the chronology and geography lenses date the Wookey pupil-teachership to 1879 (the geography lens to October 1879), on Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells'. That strains against the same article's placing him at Morley's Academy until 1880 and at Windsor in 1880. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved; the stop is ordered first because the sources date it first.
stops.campa: At twelve or thirteen he is sent into Somerset to be a pupil-teacher at the National School in Wookey, under the Mendip hills: a boy paid a little to teach boys slightly younger, studying at night for the certificate that would make it a trade. The post does not last. He is back in Kent within months, having discovered that he can stand in front of a room and hold it. Why the post ended is not recorded. The sources that date it to 1879 also keep him at Morley's until 1880, and the contradiction stands where they leave it.
suggested_refs: The National School at Wookey, Somerset

stops.name: Windsor, Rodgers and Denyer
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. The Windsor drapery is carried by the geography lens on Wells's own Experiment in Autobiography and on Sherborne, H.G. Wells: Another Kind of Life (2010); it is not in the chronology lens and does not appear in the Wikipedia article, so it rests on the biographies alone.
stops.campa: His mother, by now housekeeper at Uppark, arranges what a servant's son is supposed to want: a respectable apprenticeship in the drapery trade, at Rodgers and Denyer in Windsor under the castle walls. He lasts weeks. He is careless with the money and bad at the deference the counter requires, and he is let go. What he has seen from the first morning is the shape of the bargain: a dormitory over the shop, and a bond of years signed by a boy who cannot legally get out of it. Wells's own memoir and Sherborne carry this place. No other account read mentions it at all.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
Michael Sherborne, H.G. Wells: Another Kind of Life (2010)
suggested_refs: Rodgers and Denyer, drapers, Windsor

stops.name: Midhurst, Cowap's counter and the grammar school bench
stops.date_confidence: order corrected, month inferred. The chronology lens placed the chemist and the grammar school after the Southsea drapery, in 1883; Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' states the reverse, that a short apprenticeship at a Midhurst chemist and an even shorter stay as a boarder at Midhurst Grammar School came before he signed his papers at Hyde's. The geography lens dated the boarding to 1881, which the same passage rules out. Both lenses are corrected here to c. 1880; the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He is placed next with Samuel Cowap, chemist, in the little Sussex town of Midhurst, and this one he likes: the Latin names, the scales, the drawers of powders. It ends over money. A qualified chemist needs Latin, the Latin means the grammar school across the way, and the fee for the examination is beyond his mother's wages at Uppark. He boards at the grammar school for a short while and is pulled out again. Wikipedia calls the apprenticeship short and the boarding shorter, and dates neither. The fee is never paid.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: Samuel Cowap's chemist shop, Midhurst, West Sussex

stops.name: Southsea, Hyde's Drapery Emporium
stops.date_confidence: start year attested, month a placeholder. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' gives 'From 1880 to 1883, Wells had an unhappy apprenticeship as a draper at Hyde's Drapery Emporium in Southsea'. The geography lens headed this entry 1881-1883 and its own note corrects it to 1880, agreeing with the chronology lens; the two lenses are reconciled here on 1880.
stops.campa: Edwin Hyde's emporium in Southsea takes him on: thirteen-hour days on the shop floor, a dormitory over the stock, folding and unfolding cloth for women who will not buy it. He is fourteen when he signs and sixteen when he breaks it off. He hates the trade with a completeness that lasts the rest of his life, and it furnishes Kipps with its entire physical world, down to the smell of the counter. He walks out with no permission to go and no prospect to go to. None of the money the indenture was supposed to earn him is ever paid.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: Hyde's Drapery Emporium, King's Road, Southsea
Kipps: The Story of a Simple Soul (1905), the shop-floor chapters

stops.name: Midhurst Grammar School, the pupil-teacher returns
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. Both lenses agree that Wells returned to Midhurst Grammar School as a pupil-teacher in 1883 and that this is what got him out of the drapery. The scholarship examination result is dated to 1884 by the chronology lens.
stops.campa: He writes to Midhurst and asks to come back, this time as a pupil-teacher, paid a small salary to drill the lower forms. The school takes him. It is the third time the town has taken him in and the first time it pays him. He reads for the South Kensington science examinations at night and passes them well enough that a scholarship falls out of the result. It is a guinea a week to study biology in London. He is seventeen when he takes it, and the door he has got out of the counter by is an examination paper.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: Midhurst Grammar School, West Sussex

stops.name: South Kensington, the Normal School of Science
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder for the start of the academic year. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' dates the scholarship to 1884 and the departure without a degree to 1887; the geography lens gives the span 1884-1887. The chronology lens gives the coordinate 51.4988, -0.1749 and the geography lens 51.4966, -0.1722; the latter is used here and the discrepancy, about 350 m, is recorded.
stops.campa: On a guinea a week he enters the Normal School of Science in South Kensington and is put, in his first year, in front of Thomas Henry Huxley: the anatomist who had fought Charles Darwin's case in public for twenty years and would rather teach it than defend it again. Wells dissects, draws, and takes a first in zoology. He will call it for the rest of his life the most educative year he ever had. The second and third years are physics and geology under other men. He lets them slide, the money runs out, and he leaves in 1887 without a degree.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: The Normal School of Science, later the Royal College of Science, South Kensington
Wells's presidency of the Royal College of Science Association, 1909

stops.name: Holt, near Wrexham: the academy and the injured kidney
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' says only 'Holt Academy in Wales' and does not corroborate the football-pitch injury, which rests on Smith, H.G. Wells: Desperately Mortal (1986). The geography lens pinned this at Wrexham town centre (53.0466, -2.9931); Holt is a village about eight kilometres north-east, and the Nominatim point for Holt, Wrexham (53.0785, -2.8824) is used instead.
stops.campa: He leaves South Kensington without a degree and takes what a man without a degree can take: a post at Holt Academy in the village of Holt, near Wrexham, a school so poor that it teaches its own pupils badly. On the football pitch a boy fouls him and something inside him tears. A kidney is crushed, he passes blood, and he is carried out of Wales an invalid at twenty-one. The lung trouble that will twice more come close to killing him starts in the same season. Wikipedia places him at Holt and says nothing more; the pitch and the kidney rest on Smith alone.
sources: David C. Smith, H.G. Wells: Desperately Mortal (1986)
suggested_refs: Holt Academy, Holt, near Wrexham

stops.name: Uppark, the housekeeper's son in the library
stops.date_confidence: attested as a winter convalescence, dated 1887-1888 by the geography lens on Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' and Wikipedia, 'Uppark'. The month is a placeholder inside that winter.
stops.campa: His mother has been housekeeper at Uppark on the South Downs since he was a boy, and the sick son is allowed to convalesce below stairs through the winter. Above stairs is a library nobody uses. He reads Plato's Republic and Voltaire in a great house where he is not a guest. He is twenty-one, out of work, and nobody below stairs requires anything of him until spring. In an attic he finds a disused telescope, carries it up, and turns it on the winter sky over the Downs.
suggested_refs: The library and attic of Uppark, South Harting, West Sussex

stops.name: Henley House School, Kilburn
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to 01. The chronology lens dates the Henley House post to 1889; the geography lens gives 1889-1890. Both name A. A. Milne as a pupil, on Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells'.
stops.campa: He recovers enough to teach again, at Henley House School in Kilburn, a small private school in north-west London where a master is left to run his own classroom. Wells starts a school magazine there and puts a boy named Alan Alexander Milne to work on it. It is the last school he ever teaches in. He works by day and writes at night now, textbook chapters and journalism for the London weeklies, and he starts signing the journalism instead of sending it out anonymous.
suggested_refs: Henley House School, Mortimer Road, Kilburn

stops.name: London, the zoology degree and the cousin he marries
stops.date_confidence: years attested, months unknown and defaulted to 01. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' dates the external University of London BSc in zoology to 1890 and the marriage to Isabel Mary Wells to 1891; this stop is dated on the marriage. No source consulted gives a London address for the couple.
stops.campa: He takes a Bachelor of Science in zoology through the University of London's external programme, the route left open to men who cannot afford to be resident students. The following season he marries his cousin Isabel Mary Wells, whom he has known since childhood and courted through the drapery years. They set up in London lodgings at an address no source consulted records. He is twenty-five, has a degree and a wife, and is writing textbook chapters for money. The marriage lasts three years.
suggested_refs: The University of London external BSc, the degree route open to non-resident students

stops.name: London, the blood and the break
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to 01. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' dates the separation from Isabel and the start of life with Amy Catherine Robbins to 1894, and the two-volume Text-Book of Biology to 1893. The haemorrhage is attested in Wells's own Experiment in Autobiography; the sources do not fix its month.
stops.campa: His lungs fail again; a haemorrhage puts him in bed and convinces him he is dying, which is the condition under which he begins writing fiction in earnest. In the same stretch of months he leaves Isabel for Amy Catherine Robbins, a science student out of a class he had been teaching. She will keep his manuscripts and his accounts for the next thirty-three years, and put up with the other women under an arrangement she never publicly complains of. Her name is Amy. He calls her Jane.
sources: H. G. Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934)
suggested_refs: Text-Book of Biology, 2 vols. (1893), Wells's first book

stops.name: London, The New Review: the machine that goes along time
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Time Machine was serialised in The New Review January to May 1895 and published by Henry Holt on 7 May and by Heinemann on 29 May 1895; its precursor essays ran in The National Observer between 17 March and 23 June 1894. The chronology lens placed the book at Woking, which the dates rule out: Wells did not move to Woking until May 1895. The correction is why this stop sits in London and not on Maybury Road.
stops.campa: The New Review begins running, in monthly parts from January, a story he has been rewriting since his student magazine days: a man builds a machine that travels along time the way a bicycle travels along a road, and rides it into the year 802,701, where the human race has split into two species and one of them eats the other. The word for the device does not exist before this book. Reviewers reach for Jules Verne, who has owned this territory for thirty years. Holt publishes in New York on the seventh of May and Heinemann in London on the twenty-ninth.
stops.quote: There are really four dimensions, three which we call the three planes of Space, and a fourth, Time.
stops.quote_source: The Time Machine (1895), Chapter I; Project Gutenberg e-text #35
suggested_refs: The New Review, January to May 1895
Jorge Luis Borges, 'El primer Wells', in Otras inquisiciones (1952), arguing the early romances above the later utopian fiction

stops.name: Woking, 141 Maybury Road: the house called Lynton
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' has the move to Woking in May 1895 and the marriage at the St Pancras register office in October 1895; the chronology lens inverted the two and is corrected here. The chronology lens also pinned Woking at 51.3168, -0.5602, which is the railway station; 51.3241, -0.5426 is on Maybury Road and is used instead. The Island of Doctor Moreau was published in April 1896, while the household was still at this address, not at Worcester Park as the chronology lens had it.
stops.campa: In May, on the money the romances are starting to make, he and Jane rent a small house on Maybury Road in Woking called Lynton, and in October they marry at the St Pancras register office. The year at Woking is the most productive of his life. The Wheels of Chance and The Wonderful Visit are written here; The Invisible Man and The War of the Worlds are begun here. The Island of Doctor Moreau, about a man who makes people out of animals and cannot make them stay people, is finished in this house and published in April 1896.
sources: Michael Sherborne, H.G. Wells: Another Kind of Life (2010)
suggested_refs: The house at 141 Maybury Road, Woking
The Island of Doctor Moreau (April 1896)

stops.name: Horsell Common, the sandpit
stops.date_confidence: attested as a habit, not as an event; the geography lens dates his walks on the common to 1895-1896 on Sherborne (2010) and the month here is a placeholder. The lens coordinate 51.3295, -0.5735 lay about 1.3 km west of the common; the sandpit associated with the Martian cylinder is nearer 51.3345, -0.5605, which is used.
stops.campa: He bicycles out of Woking most days across Horsell Common, sandpits and gorse and heather on the edge of the town, and decides to destroy it. He works street by street off the map: Woking, Byfleet, Weybridge, Shepperton, Richmond, the whole line of the Thames valley into London, each place named exactly and then wrecked exactly. In the novel taking shape the first Martian cylinder falls here, into the sandpit, and the crowd that gathers at the rim to look at it is burned where it stands by a beam of heat.
stops.quote: Yet across the gulf of space, minds that are to our minds as ours are to those of the beasts that perish, intellects vast and cool and unsympathetic, regarded this earth with envious eyes, and slowly and surely drew their plans against us.
stops.quote_source: The War of the Worlds (1898), Book I, Chapter 1; Project Gutenberg e-text #36
sources: Michael Sherborne, H.G. Wells: Another Kind of Life (2010)
suggested_refs: The sandpits of Horsell Common, Woking
Michael Condron's Martian tripod sculpture, Crown Square, Woking, installed April 1998

stops.name: Worcester Park, the larger house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' places the move to Worcester Park in late summer 1896; the geography lens gives the span 1896-1898. The month is inferred from 'late summer' and defaulted within it.
stops.campa: The Woking house is too small and the income is no longer small, so the household moves to a larger one at Worcester Park, nearer Kingston upon Thames. Wells is thirty and has published five books in three years. Jane types the manuscripts, keeps the accounts, and manages a correspondence that is already a second career. He has stopped being a science teacher who writes and become a writer who used to teach science. Two years in this house produce The Invisible Man, The War of the Worlds and When the Sleeper Wakes.
suggested_refs: Heatherlea, Worcester Park, Surrey

stops.name: Worcester Park, Pearson's Magazine: the Martians land
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'The War of the Worlds' has the serial running in Pearson's Magazine from April to December 1897, with the Heinemann book edition following in 1898. The chronology lens collapsed serial and book into 1898 and is corrected here; the afterlife lens separately dated the novel to 1897, which is right for the serial and wrong for the book.
stops.campa: Pearson's Magazine begins the serial in April and runs it to December; Heinemann issues the book the following year. The premise is the one his training gives him and his contemporaries do not have: that England is not the observer of the universe but a specimen inside it, watched by something with better instruments and no scruples. The Martians land in Surrey because Surrey is where he lives. The artilleryman, the curate and the narrator's brother walk out of towns he can name street by street from his own bicycle.
stops.quote: No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man's and yet as mortal as his own.
stops.quote_source: The War of the Worlds (1898), Book I, Chapter 1, opening lines; Project Gutenberg e-text #36
suggested_refs: Pearson's Magazine, April to December 1897
The Heinemann first edition, 1898

stops.name: Worcester Park, The Invisible Man
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. Both lenses date The Invisible Man to 1897 and place its writing at Worcester Park; neither gives a publication month.
stops.campa: A book of two hundred pages about a man who solves a problem and is destroyed by the solution. Griffin, an albino medical student, refracts himself out of visibility and finds that invisibility is useless. He cannot eat without showing the food, cannot walk in snow or rain, cannot be seen to be owed anything by anybody. On the road he presses a tramp named Thomas Marvel into service and tells him what the power is for. It is a comedy for a hundred pages and a manhunt for the rest.
stops.quote: An invisible man is a man of power.
stops.quote_source: The Invisible Man (1897), Chapter IX, Griffin coercing the tramp Thomas Marvel into becoming his helper; Project Gutenberg e-text #5230
suggested_refs: The Invisible Man (1897), Chapter IX

stops.name: Sandgate, Spade House
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to 01. The chronology lens gave 51.0819, 1.1497, about 800 m off; Wikipedia, 'Spade House' gives 51.0747, 1.1525, which the geography lens also uses and which is adopted here. The geography lens dates the residence 1901-1909.
stops.campa: Doctors send him to the coast for his lungs and he stays nine years. He commissions Charles Voysey to build a house on the slope above Sandgate, looking over the Channel toward France, and overrules the architect on one point: Voysey signs his houses with a heart carved into the door furniture, and Wells wants a spade. It becomes Spade House. Here he stops being a writer of romances and starts being a public man with a programme, and Kipps, Tono-Bungay and Ann Veronica are written in the house. Both his sons by Jane are born here, George Philip in 1901 and Frank Richard in 1903.
suggested_refs: Spade House, Radnor Cliff Crescent, Sandgate, near Folkestone
Kipps (1905), Tono-Bungay (1909) and Ann Veronica (1909), all written in this house

stops.name: Rye, Lamb House: the quarrel with Henry James
stops.date_confidence: decade only. The geography lens dates the Lamb House visits to c.1900s on Sherborne (2010) and gives no year for any single visit; 1902 is a placeholder chosen inside the Spade House years. The public rupture is dated 1915 by the same lens. The lens coordinate 50.9515, 0.7278 was about 370 m off and is replaced with the Nominatim point for Lamb House, West Street, Rye.
stops.campa: Henry James is twenty-three years older, lives at Lamb House in Rye along the same stretch of coast, and takes an interest in the younger man that is at first entirely generous. They visit, they write, they disagree politely and then less politely about what a novel is for. James holds that it is for the rendering of consciousness and that Wells is squandering a gift on pamphlets. Wells holds that a novel is a tool and that James has polished his until it will not cut. The quarrel goes public in 1915 and the friendship does not survive it.
sources: Michael Sherborne, H.G. Wells: Another Kind of Life (2010)
suggested_refs: Lamb House, West Street, Rye, East Sussex
The James-Wells correspondence of 1915, and Boon (1915)

stops.name: Sandgate, A Modern Utopia
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'A Modern Utopia' gives publication by Chapman and Hall in April 1905, after serialisation in the Fortnightly Review from October 1904 to April 1905. Verne's death at Amiens on 24 March 1905 is attested; his remark distinguishing his own method from Wells's comes from the Gordon Jones interview conducted in 1903 and printed in Temple Bar, June 1904. No meeting between the two men is attested in any source consulted, and none is claimed here.
stops.campa: He publishes the book that turns the romances into a programme: a planetary state, no frontiers, land and power held in common, administered by a voluntary order of ascetics he calls the samurai. He has read Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward and found its Boston too smug, a finished thing, and insists his own utopia be kinetic, a stage and not a state. In Amiens that same March Jules Verne dies, having told an interviewer that his own inventions rest on fact where the Englishman merely invents. Chapman and Hall publish in April.
stops.quote: The Modern Utopia must be not static but kinetic, must shape not as a permanent state but as a hopeful stage, leading to a long ascent of stages.
stops.quote_source: A Modern Utopia (1905), Chapter I; Project Gutenberg e-text #6424
sources: Gordon Jones, 'Jules Verne at Home', Temple Bar, June 1904
suggested_refs: The Fortnightly Review, October 1904 to April 1905
E. M. Forster, 'The Machine Stops' (1909), written as a satire on the book's conformism

stops.name: The White House, Theodore Roosevelt
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. The geography lens dates the first American tour and the Roosevelt audience to 1906 on Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' and Smith, H.G. Wells: Desperately Mortal (1986); neither gives a month or a day for the meeting.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic to look at the United States and write it down, and the book that comes out of the trip is called The Future in America. In Washington, Theodore Roosevelt receives him at the White House, and they argue about whether the American future is a thing that can be steered or only ridden. Wells finds the country enormous, wasteful and unfinished, and the finding does not depress him. Neither of the sources that carry the audience gives a day for it inside the year 1906.
stops.quote: We build now not citadels, but ships of state.
stops.quote_source: A Modern Utopia (1905), Chapter I; Project Gutenberg e-text #6424
sources: David C. Smith, H.G. Wells: Desperately Mortal (1986)
suggested_refs: The Future in America: A Search After Realities (1906)

stops.name: Clement's Inn, the Fabian quarrel and the Reeves scandal
stops.date_confidence: years attested, month a placeholder. The geography lens dates his Fabian membership 1903-1908 and the resignation to 1908; the chronology lens dates the birth of his daughter by Amber Reeves to December 1909 and Ann Veronica to 1909. This one stop carries a span, dated on the resignation.
stops.campa: He joins the Fabian Society and immediately tries to take it over, arguing that a debating club of a few hundred should become a mass movement with a press and a programme. George Bernard Shaw and the Webbs, who built the thing, take him apart in committee, and in 1908 he resigns. The next year the society has him back in a different way. His daughter by Amber Reeves, a Fabian's daughter and his former student, is born in December 1909. Ann Veronica appears the same year. Its heroine does what Amber did and is not punished for it, and the reviewers call the book a poison.
suggested_refs: The Fabian Society offices at Clement's Inn, London
Ann Veronica (1909) and the reviews that called it a poison

segments.name: Russia, the War, and Easton Glebe

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the first Russian journey
stops.date_confidence: attested to the months, with a name corrected. Both lenses date the visit to January-February 1914 and both call the city Petrograd, following Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells'. That is an anachronism: the city was Saint Petersburg until it was renamed in August or September 1914, after the war began. The coordinate 59.9343, 30.3351 is correct and is carried unchanged. The Moscow leg of the same trip is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: He goes east in January to see Russia for the first time, spending weeks in Saint Petersburg and then Moscow as the guest of writers and reformers, and comes home describing himself as a staunch Russophile. The city is still Saint Petersburg while he walks it. The war that renames it Petrograd is seven months away. He will come back twice, once into a famine and once into the machinery of a state that does not exist on this visit, and both times he will be received as a friend.
suggested_refs: The renaming of Saint Petersburg to Petrograd, August-September 1914

stops.name: Easton Glebe, Little Easton: The World Set Free
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested, month a placeholder. The geography lens dates the Easton Glebe tenancy c.1910-1928, leased from Frances Greville, Countess of Warwick. Its coordinate 51.8814, 0.3958 was about 4.5 km east of the village; Nominatim puts Little Easton at 51.8878, 0.3242 and the church, beside which the Glebe stands, at roughly 51.8890, 0.3315, which is used here.
stops.campa: He has leased Easton Glebe, a former rectory in Essex, from the Countess of Warwick, and it is his country base for eighteen years: tennis on the lawn, weekend parties, and the desk. Here he writes a novel in which physicists learn to release the energy locked in the atom, cities burn under bombs that go on burning for years, and the survivors assemble a world government out of what is left. He calls the bombs atomic bombs, and the phrase does not exist before he writes it down. The book is published in 1914, months before the first war begins.
suggested_refs: The World Set Free (1914)
Leo Szilard read the novel in 1932 and conceived the nuclear chain reaction on 12 September 1933; see Wikipedia, 'Leo Szilard'

stops.name: London, Crewe House: propaganda against Germany
stops.date_confidence: building corrected, month a placeholder. The chronology lens placed Wells at Wellington House in 1918; Wikipedia, 'Wellington House' has the War Propaganda Bureau established on 5 September 1914 and dissolved in February 1918. His 1918 work was at Crewe House, under Lord Northcliffe, in the Department of Propaganda in Enemy Countries, from which he resigned that July. No coordinate for Crewe House was established from the research pool, so the generic London pin is used and the address is named in the campa rather than pinned.
stops.campa: The war he has been describing for twenty years arrives, and he writes a pamphlet calling it the war that will end war, a phrase that will be quoted back at him for the rest of his life. By 1918 he is inside the apparatus: at Crewe House in Mayfair, under Lord Northcliffe, directing propaganda aimed at Germany and drafting terms of a peace that would leave a league of nations standing behind it. He resigns in July, months before the fighting stops, over the government's refusal to state any war aim it could be held to afterwards.
suggested_refs: Crewe House, Curzon Street, seat of the Department of Propaganda in Enemy Countries
The War That Will End War (1914)

stops.name: Petrograd, Gorky's apartment in the famine
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. The geography lens places the 1920 lodging with Maxim Gorky in Petrograd on Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells'; the chronology lens records the Budberg relationship beginning on this trip. Neither gives a date within the year.
stops.campa: He returns in the autumn, three years into the revolution and in the middle of a famine, and lodges in Petrograd with Maxim Gorky. The city he walked in 1914 is starving. Shops are boarded, the trams have stopped, and men he knew are selling their libraries by the shelf. In Gorky's flat he meets Moura Budberg, who is Gorky's mistress and acts as Wells's interpreter. She becomes his lover on this trip and stays until he dies. He asks her to marry him for twenty-six years and she says no every time.
suggested_refs: Russia in the Shadows (1920)
Maxim Gorky's Petrograd apartment, Kronverksky Prospekt

stops.name: The Kremlin, the dreamer in the Kremlin
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. Both lenses date the Lenin interview to 1920 and credit Gorky with arranging it; neither gives a date within the year. The geography lens gives the Kremlin as 55.752, 37.6175 and the chronology lens gives Moscow as 55.7558, 37.6173; the Kremlin pin is used.
stops.campa: Gorky arranges the interview. In a small office inside the Kremlin, Lenin, fifty years old and two years from his first stroke, explains to a visiting English novelist that the Bolsheviks intend to run electricity into every village in Russia and that the countryside will be transformed by wire. Wells thinks the plan a fantasy and says so to his face. He writes the man up afterwards as the dreamer in the Kremlin. The account appears the same year in a short book called Russia in the Shadows.
suggested_refs: Russia in the Shadows (1920), chapter 'The Dreamer in the Kremlin'

stops.name: Grasse, Lou Pidou
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to 01. The geography lens dates the house and the partnership with Odette Keun 1924-1933; the chronology lens gives 1924 and a coordinate of 43.6667, 6.9167, about 1 km from the geography lens value, which is the one used. The Outline of History is dated 1920 by the chronology lens and is folded into this stop as the money that paid for the house.
stops.campa: The Outline of History, two volumes carrying the whole human story from the nebula to the League of Nations, sells past two million copies and makes him rich in a way that novels never had. With Odette Keun, a Dutch writer who becomes his partner for nine years, he builds a house in the hills above Grasse. Over the fireplace he has cut the name Lou Pidou and a line saying that two lovers built it. Jane knows about Odette, as she has known about the others, and goes on managing his English affairs from Essex.
stops.quote: Human history becomes more and more a race between education and catastrophe.
suggested_refs: Lou Pidou, above Grasse, Alpes-Maritimes
The Outline of History, 2 vols. (1920)

stops.name: Little Easton, the death of Jane
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, place corrected. The chronology lens gave the place as London; Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' has Amy Catherine Jane Wells dying on 6 October 1927, aged 55, at Dunmow, Essex, that is at Easton Glebe in Little Easton, and cremated afterwards at Golders Green. The death is pinned here and the cremation is not given a separate stop.
stops.campa: Jane is found to have cancer in the spring and dies at Easton Glebe on the sixth of October, fifty-five years old. Wells is in the house. He has been unfaithful to her for almost the whole of the thirty-three years, with her knowledge and under an arrangement she accepted, and her death goes through him in a way he does not appear to have expected. She is cremated at Golders Green. He writes an account of her and has it printed privately for her friends. He gives up Easton Glebe within the year.
suggested_refs: The Book of Catherine Wells (1928), printed with Wells's memoir of his wife

stops.name: Chiltern Court, Baker Street
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to 01. The geography lens dates the Chiltern Court flat 1930-1936. The Shape of Things to Come is dated 1933 by the chronology lens and is folded into this stop; Experiment in Autobiography, 1934, belongs to the same address.
stops.campa: He takes a flat at Chiltern Court, the block above Baker Street station, and works there through the years in which the argument he has been making for thirty years stops sounding eccentric. He publishes The Shape of Things to Come, in which a second world war begins in January 1940, runs for a decade, ruins Europe, and is followed by an air dictatorship that imposes the world state by force. The real war begins in September 1939. He is wrong by twenty months and right about what the twenty months were for.
suggested_refs: Chiltern Court, Baker Street, London
The Shape of Things to Come (1933)
Experiment in Autobiography (1934)

stops.name: Madrid, Hildegart Rodriguez declines the post
stops.date_confidence: attested, retagged, date bounded not fixed. The geography lens tagged this [R] and hedged that the contact may have been by correspondence; Wikipedia, 'Hildegart Rodriguez Carballeira' states that she accompanied Wells on a visit he made to Madrid and declined his offer to move to London as his secretary, which makes it an in-person meeting. Her mother shot her on 9 June 1933, so the visit falls before that date; no source consulted narrows it further, and 1932 is a placeholder inside the bound.
stops.campa: He goes to Madrid while the Second Spanish Republic is still standing, and among the people who take him about the city is Hildegart Rodriguez Carballeira: nineteen years old, a qualified lawyer, a writer on sexual reform, and the deliberate product of a mother who had conceived her to be a prodigy and raised her to a schedule. Wells offers her a post in London as his secretary. She declines it. On the ninth of June 1933 her mother shoots her dead while she is asleep.
suggested_refs: Hildegart Rodriguez Carballeira's writings on sexual reform, Madrid, 1930-1933

stops.name: Bridgeport, Tongue Point: the Dymaxion car
stops.date_confidence: attested. Pin, date and event inherited unchanged from buckminster_fuller.journey.json, whose own stop for the founding of the Dymaxion Corporation at the shuttered Locomobile plant records that Amelia Earhart and H. G. Wells came to ride in the car and that the newsreels swarmed. Roosevelt's bank holiday falls on the same day.
stops.campa: In the shuttered Locomobile plant at Tongue Point, Buckminster Fuller has built a three-wheeled, teardrop-bodied land craft that steers from the rear, turns inside its own length and carries eleven people. Wells comes to Bridgeport to ride in it, and Amelia Earhart comes the same day. In Washington that morning the new president has closed every bank in the United States. Wells is sixty-six and has spent forty years describing machines nobody could yet build. He gets into this one, and the newsreel cameras run.
suggested_refs: The surviving Dymaxion car prototype and the National Air and Space Museum replica

stops.name: Berlin, Opernplatz: the books burn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The chronology lens dates the Opernplatz burning to 10 May 1933 and the German library ban to the same year, on Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells'. Wells was not present; this is his work at the place, not the man, and the stop is written accordingly.
stops.campa: On the tenth of May students of the German Student Union pile books in the square between the opera house and the university and set them alight. Wells is among the authors burned, and his entire body of work is struck from German libraries in the same year. He is not in Germany. He learns of it from the newspapers, in a month when he is about to take the presidency of an international writers' organisation and has begun to understand that the century will not be argued into behaving itself.
suggested_refs: The Bebelplatz, formerly Opernplatz, Berlin, and the sunken-library memorial in its paving

stops.name: London, PEN International: the German club expelled
stops.date_confidence: presidency dates in conflict. Wikipedia, 'PEN International' gives Wells's presidency as 1932-1935; Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' gives October 1933 to October 1936. Both are recorded; this stop is dated on the later start and the conflict is not resolved. PEN's founding at the Florence Restaurant in London on 5 October 1921, with Galsworthy in the chair and Conrad, Shaw and Wells present, is attested, but no source consulted gives the restaurant a street address, so the geography lens pin of 51.5133, -0.1315 for Wardour Street is dropped and the generic London pin used instead.
stops.campa: PEN was founded at a London dinner in October 1921 and Wells was in the room, with John Galsworthy in the chair and Joseph Conrad and George Bernard Shaw at the table. Now he takes the presidency himself, and the first serious thing it asks of him is a decision. The German centre has expelled its own Jewish members in order to go on operating under the new regime. Wells has the German club expelled from the international body. The vote is taken at the Dubrovnik congress. The international body loses its German membership.
suggested_refs: The PEN International charter and the minutes of the 1933 Dubrovnik congress

stops.name: The White House, Franklin Roosevelt
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. The geography lens dates the Roosevelt call to July 1934, immediately before the Moscow leg; the chronology lens gives the whole American and Soviet trip under the date of the Stalin interview, 23 July 1934. The month is used and the day left as a placeholder.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic again at sixty-seven and is received at the White House by Franklin Roosevelt, whose New Deal he reads as the nearest thing any government has yet built to the planned world he has spent his life arguing for. Roosevelt is affable and gives him time. Wells leaves convinced, as he keeps being convinced, that he has found the man who will do it. It is the second time he has been received in this building, and the first was twenty-eight years ago. Then he sails on toward Moscow to look at the other candidate.
suggested_refs: Wells's account of the 1934 American and Soviet journey in Experiment in Autobiography

stops.name: The Kremlin, three hours with Stalin
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the chronology lens, which dates the Stalin interview 23 July 1934 and its publication to the New Statesman; the geography lens agrees. The Kremlin coordinate is carried unchanged from the 1920 stop.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of July, in the Kremlin, Stalin gives him three hours. Wells argues that the world is being reorganised by engineers and administrators and that the class war is an obsolete instrument. Stalin answers that the owners will not hand anything over to anybody and that Wells has confused the technician with the man who employs him. Neither shifts. The transcript runs in the New Statesman in October, with replies from Shaw and Keynes printed alongside it.
suggested_refs: 'Stalin-Wells Talk', New Statesman and Nation, 27 October 1934, with the replies by Shaw and Keynes

segments.name: Hanover Terrace and the End of the Tether

stops.name: 13 Hanover Terrace, the last address and the World Brain
stops.date_confidence: year attested for World Brain, month unknown and defaulted to 01. Wells lived at 13 Hanover Terrace from 1936 until his death in 1946, one decade and not two as the afterlife lens asserted. Three lenses gave three different coordinates for this one house (51.5237, -0.1657; 51.5257, -0.1608; 51.5259, -0.1637). All are reconciled here to Wikipedia's figure for Hanover Terrace, 51.52805, -0.16307, rounded to 51.5281, -0.1631.
stops.campa: He buys the lease of 13 Hanover Terrace, a Nash house on the western edge of Regent's Park, and it is his address for the last ten years of his life. From here he publishes World Brain, a set of lectures proposing a permanent world encyclopaedia: every fact the species possesses, continuously revised, mechanically reproduced, and put within reach of any person anywhere on earth. He thinks microfilm will carry it. He is seventy-two, and he does not say anywhere in the lectures who is to decide what goes in.
suggested_refs: World Brain (1938), including 'The Idea of a Permanent World Encyclopaedia'
The Greater London Council blue plaque installed at 13 Hanover Terrace in 1966

stops.name: 13 Hanover Terrace, the Rights of Man and the Black Book
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown and defaulted to 01. The chronology lens dates both The Rights of Man and Wells's appearance on the SS arrest list to 1940, and records that the text later influenced the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
stops.campa: With the second war running he drafts a declaration of the rights of man, gets it into the newspapers, campaigns for it in print and on platforms, and keeps campaigning for it until he is too ill to travel; the text feeds into the declaration the United Nations adopts two years after his death. In the same year, in Berlin, the SS compiles a list of people to be arrested at once when Britain is occupied. His name is on it. He is seventy-four, living under the bombing, and refuses to leave London.
suggested_refs: The Rights of Man, or What Are We Fighting For? (1940)
The Sonderfahndungsliste G.B., the SS special search list for Great Britain

stops.name: The only meeting with Orson Welles
stops.date_confidence: month attested, place not established. Wikipedia, 'The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)' records that the two men met in person only once, in October 1940, and gives Wells's remark; no source consulted names the place. The pin is Wells's own London address and is a placeholder, not the location of the meeting, which was in the United States.
stops.campa: Two years earlier a young American had put The War of the Worlds on the radio as a run of news bulletins and been accused of terrifying a nation; historians now put the audience who heard it at about two per cent of listeners. Now the two men meet, the only time they ever do, and are put on the air together. Wells is seventy-four and not indignant about the borrowing. He wants to know whether there was ever a panic at all, or whether it was a piece of Halloween fun. Orson Welles is twenty-five.
stops.quote: Are you sure there was such a panic in America or wasn't it your Halloween fun?
stops.quote_source: H. G. Wells to Orson Welles, October 1940; Wikipedia, 'The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)'
sources: Wikipedia, 'The War of the Worlds (1938 radio drama)'

stops.name: 13 Hanover Terrace, the end of the tether
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Wikipedia, 'H. G. Wells' gives the death as 13 August 1946, aged 79, at 13 Hanover Terrace, with Mind at the End of Its Tether published in 1945. The epitaph is dated to a 1941 preface by the chronology lens; there is no stone on which it could have been cut.
stops.campa: In 1945 he publishes thirty-two pages saying that the writer can see no way out: that a hard and limiting reality has closed on human affairs, that the species has run out of the adaptability its survival requires, and that no reprieve is to be looked for. Everything he had argued for fifty years is withdrawn in them. He dies at home the following August, seventy-nine years old, Moura Budberg among those near him. He had told a publisher what he wanted on his stone: I told you so. You damned fools.
suggested_refs: Mind at the End of Its Tether (1945)

stops.name: Golders Green Crematorium
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The chronology lens gave 51.5794, -0.1969 and the afterlife lens 51.5726, -0.1936, both off by 300 to 500 m; Wikipedia, 'Golders Green Crematorium' gives 51.57722, -0.19361, which is used and which the geography lens also carried.
stops.campa: The funeral is on the sixteenth of August, at the crematorium in Golders Green where Jane had been cremated nineteen years before. The register enters him among those whose ashes were taken away rather than interred. There is no grave, no plot and no stone anywhere, and no epitaph either, though he had written one and given it to a publisher. The plaques and the one statue that will eventually mark him stand in Bromley, in Woking and on Hanover Terrace, at addresses where he lived or was born.
suggested_refs: The Golders Green Crematorium register entry recording the ashes as taken elsewhere

stops.name: Old Harry Rocks, the ashes on the water
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month a placeholder. The afterlife lens tagged the scattering [R] and doubted the location; Wikipedia, 'Old Harry Rocks' states plainly that Wells's ashes were scattered in the water off Old Harry Rocks and cites Anthony West, H. G. Wells: Aspects of a Life (Hutchinson, 1984), p. 153, so the claim is retagged attested here. Anthony West was Wells's son by Rebecca West, not his son-in-law as the geography lens had it. The lens coordinate 50.6478, -1.9163 is replaced with Wikipedia's 50.6423, -1.9236.
stops.campa: The ashes are taken to Dorset and scattered into the sea off Old Harry Rocks, three chalk stacks standing at the end of the Purbeck ridge where the cliffs run out into the water. It is the same water he had watched from the windows of Spade House for nine years, and across which he had sent his Martians and his aeroplanes and his atomic bombs. The account comes from Anthony West, his son by Rebecca West, in a biography written thirty-eight years afterwards. No source names the day. Nothing marks the place.
sources: Anthony West, H. G. Wells: Aspects of a Life (Hutchinson, 1984), p. 153
suggested_refs: Old Harry Rocks, off Studland, Dorset
Anthony West, H. G. Wells: Aspects of a Life (1984)
